questions.question: What are the three types of statements in JDBC?
questions.title: JDBC Statement Types — Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement
questions.direct_answer: JDBC has three statement types: Statement (static SQL, no parameters — avoid for user input), PreparedStatement (parameterized SQL, precompiled, prevents injection — use for all queries with parameters), CallableStatement (executes stored procedures).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of statement types and when to use each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Statement with string concatenation for user input — SQL injection vulnerability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Emphasize that PreparedStatement is always preferred for parameterized queries due to SQL injection prevention and performance

sections.title: Three Flavors of SQL Execution in JDBC
sections.content: JDBC provides three statement interfaces, each designed for different SQL execution scenarios. **Statement** is the simplest — you pass a complete SQL string with no placeholders, useful only for static queries with zero parameters. **PreparedStatement** extends Statement and lets you use **parameter placeholders** (?) in your SQL; the database precompiles the query once, then you can execute it multiple times with different values — this prevents SQL injection and boosts performance. **CallableStatement** extends PreparedStatement and is specialized for **stored procedures** — database functions that live server-side and can return output parameters. Think of it as a progression: Statement for hardcoded SQL, PreparedStatement for queries with user input, CallableStatement when business logic lives in the database. In real Spring Boot apps connecting to PostgreSQL, you'll use PreparedStatement 95% of the time because almost every query involves dynamic values like user IDs or search filters.

sections.title: All Three Statement Types in Action
Key Points
content: **Statement**: executes static SQL strings with no placeholders — vulnerable to SQL injection if you concatenate user input
**PreparedStatement**: uses ? placeholders for parameters, database precompiles the query once for performance and security
**CallableStatement**: specialized for stored procedures, supports IN/OUT/INOUT parameters with registerOutParameter()
**SQL Injection**: Statement with string concatenation allows malicious input to break out and execute arbitrary SQL
**Performance**: PreparedStatement is faster for repeated queries because the execution plan is cached on the database server
**Best Practice**: use PreparedStatement for all queries with variable values — only use Statement for admin scripts or static queries
**Spring Boot**: JdbcTemplate and Spring Data JPA abstract these statement types but use PreparedStatement under the hood

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JDBC gives you three ways to execute SQL. Statement is the basic one — you just pass a complete SQL string. It's fine for something like select count from orders where there's no user input, but you should avoid it if you're building SQL with variables because that opens you up to SQL injection. PreparedStatement is what you'd use most of the time. You write your SQL with question marks as placeholders, like select from customers where email equals question mark, then you set the actual value with setString. The database compiles that query once and reuses it, so it's both faster and secure because parameters can't break out of the SQL syntax. CallableStatement is for calling stored procedures — functions that live in the database. You use curly brace syntax like call calculate total, and you can register output parameters to get values back from the procedure. Most Spring Boot apps with PostgreSQL use PreparedStatement through JdbcTemplate or JPA, which handle the boilerplate for you. The key mistake freshers make is using Statement with string concatenation thinking it's simpler — that's how SQL injection happens. Always reach for PreparedStatement when you have dynamic values. In an interview, I'd say PreparedStatement is your default choice for any query with parameters, Statement is rare and only for hardcoded SQL, and CallableStatement is niche for when business logic lives in database stored procedures.

questions.question: Why should you avoid using Statement with string concatenation for user input?
questions.title: SQL Injection Risk with JDBC Statement
questions.direct_answer: Using Statement with string concatenation allows SQL injection — malicious user input can break out of the SQL string and execute arbitrary SQL. PreparedStatement prevents this because parameters are always treated as data values, never as SQL syntax.

interviewer_intent.testing: SQL injection risk awareness with Statement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Statement with string concatenation thinking it is safe
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete SQL injection example and explain precisely why PreparedStatement prevents it

sections.title: The SQL Injection Vulnerability in Statement
sections.content: When you use **Statement** and build SQL with string concatenation, you're mixing code and data in a dangerous way. User input becomes part of the SQL command itself. An attacker can craft input that closes the original query and appends malicious SQL — like a WHERE clause that's always true, or a DROP TABLE command. This is **SQL injection**, one of the oldest and most devastating web vulnerabilities. The root problem: the database can't distinguish between your intended SQL structure and the user's injected commands because it's all one giant string. **PreparedStatement** solves this by separating the SQL template (with ? placeholders) from the actual data values. The database receives the structure first, compiles it, then treats parameters as pure data — they can never alter the query's logic. Think of it like filling in a form with fixed fields versus letting someone rewrite the form itself. In a Spring Boot PostgreSQL app, using Statement with concatenation for user input is a critical security flaw that can lead to data breaches, data loss, or complete system compromise.

sections.title: SQL Injection Attack vs Safe PreparedStatement
Key Points
content: **SQL Injection**: attacker inserts SQL syntax into user input to alter the query's logic — possible with Statement concatenation
**Attack Example**: input like alice OR one equals one closes the string and adds a condition that's always true, bypassing authentication
**Why Statement Fails**: the database sees one big SQL string with no boundary between your code and user data
**PreparedStatement Protection**: parameters are sent separately from the SQL structure — special characters are automatically escaped
**Database Precompilation**: PreparedStatement's SQL template is parsed before parameters arrive, so parameters can never change the query structure
**OWASP Top 10**: SQL injection is consistently ranked as one of the most critical web application vulnerabilities
**Real Impact**: attackers can read sensitive data, modify or delete records, escalate privileges, or drop entire tables

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Statement with string concatenation is dangerous because user input becomes part of the SQL command. Let's say you're checking if an email exists, and you build the query like select from customers where email equals quote plus userInput plus quote. An attacker can type something like alice at example dot com quote OR quote one equals one. When you concatenate that, the database sees select from customers where email equals alice or one equals one — the OR clause is always true, so it returns every customer in the table. That's SQL injection. The attacker just rewrote your query's logic. PreparedStatement prevents this because you write the SQL with a question mark placeholder, then set the parameter separately. The database compiles the query structure first, knowing exactly where the data should go. When the parameter arrives, it's treated as a literal string value. Even if it contains quotes or SQL keywords, they're automatically escaped — they can't break out and become executable SQL. The database never interprets the parameter as code, only as data. In a production Spring Boot app, using Statement with concatenation for any user input is a critical vulnerability. The common mistake freshers make is thinking simple validation like checking for quotes is enough — attackers have dozens of ways to bypass that. The only safe approach is PreparedStatement, which makes SQL injection structurally impossible.

questions.question: What is the performance benefit of PreparedStatement over Statement?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Performance Benefits
questions.direct_answer: PreparedStatement is precompiled by the database server — the SQL is parsed and optimized once, then reused with different parameters. Statement re-parses and re-optimizes on every execution. For repeated queries with different values, PreparedStatement is significantly faster.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking PreparedStatement is only about security, not performance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain execution plan caching on the database server side

sections.title: Why PreparedStatement Is Faster Than Statement
sections.content: Every SQL query goes through multiple stages on the database server: **parsing** (breaking the SQL into a syntax tree), **planning** (choosing the optimal execution strategy — which indexes to use, join order), and **execution**. With **Statement**, the database repeats all three stages every single time because each SQL string looks brand new. With **PreparedStatement**, you send the SQL template with ? placeholders once, and the database does the parse and plan steps immediately. It stores that **execution plan** in memory, tagged to your prepared statement. When you execute with actual parameter values, the database skips straight to execution using the cached plan. This is called **query plan caching**. The performance gain is dramatic for repeated queries — think of a loop inserting 1000 orders, or a search endpoint hit thousands of times per hour. In a Spring Boot app with PostgreSQL, connection pooling amplifies this benefit: if the PreparedStatement is created once when the pool initializes, all subsequent requests reuse the same compiled query. The database does less work, and your app responds faster.

sections.title: Performance Comparison: Statement vs PreparedStatement
Key Points
content: **Query Lifecycle**: SQL execution has three phases — parse (syntax check), plan (optimization), execute (retrieve data)
**Statement Cost**: repeats parse and plan on every call because each SQL string is unique to the database
**PreparedStatement Optimization**: database compiles the SQL template once, caches the execution plan, reuses it for all executions
**Plan Cache**: the database stores the optimized query plan in memory, keyed to the PreparedStatement object
**Benefit Multiplier**: performance gain increases with query complexity (more joins, subqueries) and execution frequency
**Connection Pooling**: when PreparedStatements are reused across pooled connections, the plan cache persists across requests
**PostgreSQL Specifics**: Postgres uses server-side prepared statements after a threshold (default 5 executions), caching plan indefinitely

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: PreparedStatement is faster because the database does less work on each execution. When you run a SQL query, the database has to parse it — figure out the syntax and tables involved — then create an execution plan, which is the optimized strategy for retrieving data, like which indexes to use. With Statement, the database sees a brand new SQL string every time, so it has to do all that parsing and planning over and over. With PreparedStatement, you send the SQL template with question marks once. The database parses it immediately, builds the execution plan, and stores that plan in memory. When you execute the prepared statement with actual values, the database skips the parse and plan steps and goes straight to execution using the cached plan. That's a huge time saver, especially for complex queries or queries that run thousands of times. Let's say you're inserting a thousand orders in a loop. With Statement, the database plans the insert a thousand times. With PreparedStatement, it plans once and executes a thousand times. The more complex the query — like a multi-table join — the bigger the planning overhead you're avoiding. In a Spring Boot app with connection pooling, the PreparedStatement can be created once when the pool starts, and all requests reuse the same compiled query. The mistake freshers make is thinking PreparedStatement is only about security. It's actually a performance optimization too. If you only run a query once, the benefit is minimal, but for repeated queries with different parameters, PreparedStatement is significantly faster.

questions.question: What is CallableStatement in JDBC and when do you use it?
questions.title: CallableStatement in JDBC — Stored Procedures
questions.direct_answer: CallableStatement executes database stored procedures. Syntax: call procedure_name or equals call function_name for functions. Supports IN (input), OUT (output), and INOUT parameters. Used when business logic is in the database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of CallableStatement for stored procedures
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the stored procedure call syntax with curly braces
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain IN vs OUT vs INOUT parameters and when organizations use stored procedures

sections.title: CallableStatement for Stored Procedures
sections.content: **CallableStatement** is JDBC's interface for executing **stored procedures** — precompiled SQL routines that live on the database server. Unlike regular queries that you send from Java, stored procedures are defined once in the database (think PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL functions) and invoked by name. They can encapsulate complex business logic, return multiple result sets, and most importantly, support **output parameters** — values the procedure computes and sends back to your Java code. CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so it supports input parameters (IN), but adds **OUT parameters** (procedure sets them, you read them) and **INOUT parameters** (you send a value, procedure modifies it, you read the modified value). The syntax uses **JDBC escape notation** with curly braces: {call procedure_name(?)} for procedures, {? = call function_name(?)} for functions that return a value. In practice, stored procedures are common in legacy enterprise systems or when database-side logic (like auditing, complex calculations) is mandated. In modern Spring Boot apps, business logic usually lives in Java service classes, but you'll encounter CallableStatement when integrating with older databases or systems where the DBA team controls logic.

sections.title: Calling a Stored Procedure with OUT Parameter
Key Points
content: **Stored Procedure**: precompiled SQL routine stored in the database, encapsulates business logic server-side
**CallableStatement**: JDBC interface for executing stored procedures, extends PreparedStatement with output parameter support
**JDBC Escape Syntax**: use curly braces like call proc or equals call func — driver translates to database-specific syntax
**IN Parameter**: input you pass to the procedure, set with setInt, setString like PreparedStatement
**OUT Parameter**: value the procedure computes and returns, must call registerOutParameter before execute, read with getter methods
**INOUT Parameter**: send a value in, procedure modifies it, read modified value out — register as OUT and set as IN
**Use Cases**: complex calculations, auditing, multi-step transactions, legacy systems where logic lives in the database

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: CallableStatement is used to execute stored procedures — SQL functions that live in the database. You'd use it when business logic is implemented on the database server instead of in your Java code. The syntax is a bit different from regular SQL — you use curly braces like call calculate discount with question marks for parameters. That's called JDBC escape syntax. The big difference from PreparedStatement is that stored procedures can have output parameters. You pass inputs like normal with setLong or setString, but for outputs you have to call registerOutParameter before you execute. You tell it the parameter index and the SQL type, like Types dot DECIMAL. Then after you call execute, you read the output value with getBigDecimal or whatever matches the type. There's also INOUT parameters where you send a value in, the procedure modifies it, and you read the modified value back out. A concrete example: let's say you have a procedure that calculates an order discount based on customer tier and order total. You'd pass in the order ID as an IN parameter and register the discount amount as an OUT parameter. The procedure runs on the database, does the calculation, and sets the discount. Then you retrieve it in Java and apply it to the final price. In modern Spring Boot apps, we usually put business logic in service classes, so CallableStatement is less common. You'd see it in legacy enterprise systems or when the DBA team controls certain logic. The mistake freshers make is trying to use PreparedStatement for stored procedures — it can call them, but it can't handle output parameters, so you can't get values back.

questions.question: What is the difference between execute(), executeQuery(), and executeUpdate() in JDBC?
questions.title: execute() vs executeQuery() vs executeUpdate() in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: executeQuery(): for SELECT statements, returns ResultSet. executeUpdate(): for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL, returns affected row count as int. execute(): generic — handles any SQL, returns boolean (true if ResultSet produced). Use specific methods when you know the statement type.

interviewer_intent.testing: JDBC execution methods and their return types
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using executeQuery for an INSERT or using executeUpdate for a SELECT
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that executeUpdate on DDL (CREATE TABLE) returns 0 and that execute() is useful for dynamic SQL

sections.title: Three Ways to Execute SQL in JDBC
sections.content: JDBC statement interfaces provide three execution methods, each optimized for different SQL statement types. **executeQuery()** is for SELECT queries — it always returns a **ResultSet** containing the rows you retrieved. Use this when you're reading data and expect rows back. **executeUpdate()** is for **data modification statements** (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and **DDL statements** (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP) — it returns an **int** representing the number of rows affected. Use this when you're changing data or schema and need to know how many rows were impacted. **execute()** is the **generic method** that handles any SQL — it returns a **boolean**: true if the result is a ResultSet (like a SELECT), false if it's an update count (like an INSERT). It's useful when you don't know the statement type at compile time, such as executing user-provided SQL in an admin tool. In typical Spring Boot app code, you'll use executeQuery() for all reads and executeUpdate() for all writes. The execute() method is rare — most production code knows exactly what SQL it's running.

rows: Modifying data or schema — need affected row count
Dynamic SQL — don't know type at compile time

sections.title: Choosing the Right Execution Method
sections.content: Use **executeQuery()** for any SELECT statement where you're retrieving data. The method signature forces you to handle the ResultSet, making it clear this is a read operation. Use **executeUpdate()** for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements. The int return value tells you how many rows were affected — crucial for verifying that an UPDATE actually changed records or an INSERT succeeded. For DDL like CREATE TABLE, the return value is always 0 because DDL doesn't affect rows. Use **execute()** only when the SQL statement type is determined at runtime — for example, a database migration tool that reads SQL scripts, or an admin console that lets users run arbitrary queries. Call getResultSet() if execute() returns true, or getUpdateCount() if it returns false. In Spring Boot production code, stick to executeQuery() and executeUpdate() — they're type-safe and self-documenting.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **executeQuery()**: only for SELECT, returns ResultSet, throws SQLException if used with INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
**executeUpdate()**: for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL, returns int row count, throws SQLException if used with SELECT
**execute()**: generic method returns boolean — true means ResultSet available, false means update count available
**Row Count**: executeUpdate() returns number of affected rows — 0 for DDL or when no rows matched the WHERE clause
**Type Safety**: using specific methods prevents runtime errors — executeQuery() for a DELETE will fail at call time
**Dynamic SQL**: execute() is useful for tools that run user-provided SQL where type isn't known at compile time
**Spring JdbcTemplate**: abstracts these methods — query() for SELECT, update() for modifications, execute() for DDL

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JDBC gives you three ways to execute SQL, each suited for different statement types. executeQuery is for SELECT statements — it returns a ResultSet with the rows you retrieved. You'd use this when you're reading data from the database. If you try to call executeQuery on an INSERT or UPDATE, it'll throw an exception because those don't produce a ResultSet. executeUpdate is for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL statements like CREATE TABLE. It returns an int — the number of rows affected by the statement. For an UPDATE, that's how many rows matched your WHERE clause and got changed. For a DELETE, it's how many rows got removed. For DDL like CREATE TABLE, it always returns zero because DDL doesn't affect rows, it changes schema. If you call executeUpdate on a SELECT, you'll get an exception. execute is the generic method that handles any SQL. It returns a boolean — true if the result is a ResultSet, false if it's an update count. After calling execute, you check the return value. If it's true, you call getResultSet to retrieve the rows. If it's false, you call getUpdateCount to get the number of affected rows. You'd use execute when you don't know the statement type at compile time, like if you're building a database admin tool that runs user-provided SQL. In normal Spring Boot code, you almost always know what kind of SQL you're running, so you'd use executeQuery for reads and executeUpdate for writes. The mistake freshers make is mixing them up — calling executeQuery for an INSERT or executeUpdate for a SELECT — which throws an exception at runtime. The method names are self-documenting, so just match the method to the SQL type.

questions.question: When would you use a Statement instead of PreparedStatement?
questions.title: When to Use Statement vs PreparedStatement
questions.direct_answer: Use Statement for static, parameterless SQL that you construct entirely in code with no user input — like schema migration scripts or fixed admin queries. For any query with user-provided or variable values, always use PreparedStatement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to distinguish appropriate use cases for Statement vs PreparedStatement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Statement for queries that have variable values — a security and maintainability issue
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that in almost all application code, PreparedStatement is preferred — Statement's use is very narrow

sections.title: The Narrow Use Case for Statement
sections.content: In modern Java applications, **Statement** has an extremely limited role. You'd use it only for **completely static SQL** — queries with zero parameters, no user input, and no variable values. Think schema migration scripts that create tables, drop indexes, or run fixed administrative queries like SELECT COUNT(*) FROM all_tables. The SQL is hardcoded in your Java source, never constructed from runtime values. **PreparedStatement** is the default choice for everything else because it prevents SQL injection and improves performance. Even if your query has no user input but uses a variable like a customer ID from your session or a date from a calculation, PreparedStatement is still better — it's safer, more maintainable, and enables query plan caching. In a production Spring Boot app, Statement appears in database initialization scripts (like schema.sql execution), migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase), or developer utilities. Application business logic should use PreparedStatement or higher-level abstractions like JdbcTemplate. The rule: if there's any chance a value in your SQL came from outside the source code, it's PreparedStatement territory.

sections.title: Step 1: Check for Variable Values
sections.content: First, identify whether your SQL contains any values that change at runtime. This includes user input (search terms, form data), session data (logged-in user ID), calculated values (timestamps, order totals), or configuration (database names, table prefixes). If the answer is yes — even for one value — use **PreparedStatement**. Statement is only appropriate when every single token in your SQL string is a literal constant in your source code. Example of static SQL: CREATE TABLE orders, SELECT version(), DROP INDEX idx_customer. Example of variable SQL: SELECT * WHERE status = 'pending' — even though 'pending' is hardcoded here, if it could be 'shipped' in another code path, that's a variable, so use PreparedStatement.

sections.title: Step 2: Consider Security and Maintainability
sections.content: Even if your SQL is technically static today, ask: could this change? If a hardcoded query might later need a WHERE clause with a user filter, starting with PreparedStatement saves a rewrite. Security-wise, Statement with any string building (even concatenating constants) is a code review red flag — it signals poor practices that could propagate. Maintainability matters too: PreparedStatement makes the SQL structure explicit with ? placeholders, separating logic from data. Statement with concatenation mixes them, making code harder to audit. The **safe default rule**: unless you're writing a one-time database script or a tool that generates DDL, always use PreparedStatement. In team environments, some shops ban Statement entirely in application code to eliminate the risk of accidental misuse.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Statement Use Cases**: schema DDL (CREATE, DROP), fixed admin queries (SELECT count), database metadata queries (SHOW TABLES)
**PreparedStatement Default**: use for all queries with parameters, user input, session data, or calculated values
**Security Rule**: if any part of the SQL could originate outside source code, PreparedStatement is mandatory
**Performance**: even for static SQL, PreparedStatement enables plan caching if the query runs multiple times
**Code Review**: Statement with string concatenation is an automatic rejection in security-conscious teams
**Spring Boot Tools**: Flyway and Liquibase use Statement internally for migrations but those are controlled scripts, not user-facing code
**Best Practice**: treat PreparedStatement as the default JDBC execution method — Statement is the rare exception

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You'd use Statement only for completely static SQL where every part of the query is hardcoded in your source code with zero parameters. Think database initialization scripts — like creating a table with CREATE TABLE orders or dropping an index with DROP INDEX. The SQL is fixed, you're not plugging in any values, and there's no user input involved. Another example is running a metadata query like SELECT version to check the database version. For everything else, you should use PreparedStatement. Even if the query seems static, like SELECT from customers WHERE status equals active, if that status value could change — maybe it's shipped in another code path — use PreparedStatement. The rule is: if any value in the SQL comes from outside your source code — user input, session data, a config file, a calculation — it's PreparedStatement territory. That covers 99 percent of application code. In a Spring Boot app, you'd see Statement in tools like Flyway that run migration scripts, or in developer utilities that generate DDL. But in business logic — controllers, services, repositories — it's always PreparedStatement or higher abstractions like JdbcTemplate. The mistake freshers make is thinking Statement is simpler for one-off queries. It's not worth the risk. Even if you're 100 percent sure there's no user input today, someone might modify the code tomorrow and concatenate a variable, introducing SQL injection. PreparedStatement is safer, often faster due to plan caching, and more maintainable because the SQL structure is explicit. In an interview, I'd say PreparedStatement is my default choice — Statement's use case is so narrow that in most apps, you'd never write one outside of database scripts.

questions.question: How does PreparedStatement's precompilation improve performance?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Precompilation and Performance
questions.direct_answer: When PreparedStatement is created, the database parses and compiles the SQL into an execution plan once. Subsequent executions reuse that plan, skipping the parse-compile step. This is especially beneficial when the same parameterized query runs many times.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of database query processing stages — not just that PreparedStatement is fast, but why
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking precompilation helps when you only run a PreparedStatement once — it only helps on repeated executions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention server-side vs client-side prepared statements and that connection pooling amplifies the benefit when the PS is created once per pool

sections.title: Database Query Processing and Plan Caching
sections.content: When a database executes SQL, it goes through distinct stages: **parsing** (lexical and syntax analysis — is this valid SQL?), **semantic analysis** (do these tables and columns exist?), **optimization** (choosing indexes, join order, access paths — the execution plan), and finally **execution** (retrieving or modifying data). With **Statement**, every SQL string is unique, so the database repeats all four stages on each call. With **PreparedStatement**, you send the SQL template with ? placeholders once. The database performs parse, semantic check, and optimization immediately, storing the resulting **execution plan** in memory. This is **precompilation**. On subsequent executions, you send only the parameter values, and the database jumps straight to execution using the cached plan. The performance benefit grows with query complexity (more joins, subqueries) and execution frequency (a search endpoint hit 10,000 times per day). In a Spring Boot app with **connection pooling**, the effect is amplified: create the PreparedStatement once when the connection is established, and all requests through that pooled connection reuse the same compiled query. PostgreSQL specifically uses **server-side prepared statements** after a threshold (default 5 executions), caching the plan on the server for the connection's lifetime.

sections.title: Precompilation Lifecycle with Connection Pooling
Key Points
content: **Precompilation**: database parses and optimizes PreparedStatement SQL once, stores execution plan in memory
**Execution Plan**: database's strategy for retrieving data — which indexes to use, join order, access methods
**Plan Cache**: optimized plan is keyed to the PreparedStatement object, reused on every execution with different parameters
**Performance Gain**: skip parse and optimization on subsequent executions — significant for complex queries or high frequency
**Server-Side Prepared Statements**: PostgreSQL promotes to server-side after threshold (default 5 executions), caching plan on server
**Connection Pooling**: PreparedStatement created once per pooled connection, all requests through that connection reuse the plan
**One-Time Queries**: if you create and execute a PreparedStatement once, precompilation overhead may slightly increase latency — benefit is in reuse

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: PreparedStatement's precompilation improves performance by letting the database do the expensive work once and reuse it. When you execute SQL, the database has to parse it — check the syntax and figure out what tables and columns you're referencing — then build an execution plan, which is the optimized strategy for getting the data. That planning step is costly, especially for complex queries with joins or subqueries. With Statement, the database sees a brand new SQL string every time, so it re-parses and re-plans on every call. With PreparedStatement, you send the SQL template with question marks once. The database immediately parses it and builds the execution plan, then stores that plan in memory. When you execute the prepared statement later with actual parameter values, the database skips the parse and plan steps and goes straight to execution using the cached plan. That's the precompilation benefit — the database does less work on each execution. The performance gain increases with how often you run the query. If you create a PreparedStatement and execute it once, the benefit is minimal — you actually pay a tiny overhead for the precompilation. But if you execute it a thousand times, you're saving the parse and plan cost 999 times. In a Spring Boot app with connection pooling, the effect is amplified. The PreparedStatement is created once when the connection is initialized, and all requests through that pooled connection reuse the same compiled query. PostgreSQL takes this further — after you execute a PreparedStatement five times on the same connection, it promotes it to a server-side prepared statement and caches the plan permanently for that connection. So the plan sticks around across requests. The mistake freshers make is thinking precompilation is a magic bullet. It only helps with repeated executions. But in real apps, that's most queries — think a search endpoint or an order insert that runs constantly. That's where PreparedStatement's performance benefit shines.

questions.question: How do you execute a stored procedure with JDBC?
questions.title: Executing Stored Procedures in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Use CallableStatement with prepareCall() and the JDBC escape syntax call procedure_name. Register output parameters with registerOutParameter before calling execute, then read them with the typed getter methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with the three Statement types and the CallableStatement API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using PreparedStatement for stored procedures — it can call procedures but can't handle output parameters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the JDBC escape syntax and the Spring SimpleJdbcCall abstraction as a cleaner alternative

sections.title: Executing Stored Procedures with CallableStatement
sections.content: To execute a stored procedure from JDBC, you use **CallableStatement**, created with **connection.prepareCall()**. The SQL uses **JDBC escape syntax** — curly braces around the call keyword: {call procedure_name(?)} for procedures, {? = call function_name(?)} for functions that return a value. The question marks are parameter placeholders, just like PreparedStatement. For **input parameters** (IN), you use setter methods like setLong, setString. For **output parameters** (OUT), you must call **registerOutParameter()** before executing, specifying the parameter index and SQL type (java.sql.Types). After calling execute(), you retrieve output values with typed getters like getInt, getString, getBigDecimal. If the procedure returns a result set, call getResultSet() like you would with a SELECT. In Spring Boot applications, you can use **SimpleJdbcCall**, a higher-level abstraction that automatically discovers parameter types and result set mappings, reducing boilerplate. However, understanding CallableStatement is essential because many legacy enterprise systems and database-heavy applications rely on stored procedures for business logic, and you'll need to debug or maintain that code.

sections.title: Complete CallableStatement Example with IN and OUT Parameters
Key Points
content: **prepareCall()**: creates CallableStatement, takes SQL with JDBC escape syntax like call proc_name
**JDBC Escape Syntax**: curly braces around call keyword — portable across databases, driver translates to native syntax
**IN Parameters**: set with setInt, setString, etc., just like PreparedStatement — parameter index starts at 1
**OUT Parameters**: must call registerOutParameter(index, Types.X) before execute(), retrieve with getter methods after execute()
**INOUT Parameters**: combination — call both setX() and registerOutParameter(), read modified value after execute()
**Return Values**: functions that return a value use syntax question mark equals call func — register position 1 as OUT
**Spring SimpleJdbcCall**: higher-level abstraction that auto-discovers parameters and result sets, preferred in modern Spring Boot apps

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To execute a stored procedure with JDBC, you use CallableStatement. You create it with connection dot prepareCall and pass the SQL in JDBC escape syntax — that's curly braces around the word call and the procedure name with question marks for parameters. So it looks like call calculate discount with two question marks. The question marks work like PreparedStatement — you set input parameters with setLong or setString, and the parameter index starts at one. The key difference is output parameters. If the procedure returns a value, you have to register it before you execute. You call registerOutParameter with the parameter index and the SQL type from java dot sql dot Types, like Types dot DECIMAL. Then you call execute to run the procedure. After that, you retrieve the output value with a typed getter like getBigDecimal or getString, passing the same parameter index. Let's say you have a procedure that calculates an order discount. You'd pass in the order ID with setLong at index one, register the discount amount as an OUT parameter at index two with Types dot DECIMAL, call execute, then read the discount with getBigDecimal at index two. If the procedure returns a result set, you'd call getResultSet after execute, just like a SELECT query. There's also INOUT parameters where you set a value, the procedure modifies it, and you read it back — you call both the setter and registerOutParameter for the same index. In modern Spring Boot apps, there's a cleaner way called SimpleJdbcCall. It's a Spring abstraction that automatically discovers the procedure's parameters and result sets, so you don't have to manually register outputs. You just pass a map of parameter names and values, and it handles the JDBC boilerplate. But understanding CallableStatement is still important for legacy systems or when you need fine control. The mistake freshers make is trying to use PreparedStatement for stored procedures. It can execute the call, but it can't handle output parameters, so you can't retrieve values the procedure returns. CallableStatement is the right tool for procedures.

beats.text: Executing a stored procedure means using CallableStatement with a special JDBC escape syntax, registering any output parameters before calling execute(), then reading the outputs afterwards.

The JDBC escape syntax {call proc(?, ?)} is database-agnostic. The driver translates it into the native call syntax for MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Oracle, so your Java code doesn't change between databases.

items: prepareCall('{call proc_name(?, ?)}') — creates the CallableStatement with JDBC escape syntax
setXxx(position, value) — sets IN parameters, same as PreparedStatement
registerOutParameter(position, Types.XXX) — declares an OUT parameter before execute()
execute() — runs the procedure; use this, not executeQuery or executeUpdate
getXxx(position) — reads the OUT parameter value after execute()

beats.text: A MySQL stored procedure archive_old_orders takes a cutoff date as IN and returns archived_count as OUT. Java: prepareCall('{call archive_old_orders(?, ?)}'), setDate(1, cutoff), registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER), execute(), then getInt(2) gives the count. Spring's SimpleJdbcCall does the same thing with less code: new SimpleJdbcCall(dataSource).withProcedureName('archive_old_orders').execute(mapOf cutoff). Using executeQuery() on a procedure that returns no ResultSet — use execute() for procedures regardless.
